en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Building Stūpas to Prolong Life, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Prajña of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
King Prasenajit was present in that great assembly;
he then rose from his seat and adjusted his robes.
Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee on the ground,
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
An astrologer has predicted for me that after seven days have passed,"
My life must surely come to an end;
I am oppressed by the suffering of impermanence and have come to take refuge in the World-Honored One, having no other support or reliance.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will protect and deliver me.
How may I be freed from this sorrow and suffering?
The Buddha replied:
"Great King, please comfort yourself; do not be anxious or afraid.
The Tathāgatas possess skillful means that can enable Your Majesty to obtain extraordinary benefits and extend your lifespan."
When you shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Great King, you should know that if you wish to escape impermanence and suffering and transcend into the lifespan of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body,
you should first resolve to uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts and cultivate the highest merit.
"By being able to give rise to this mind, one can prolong the king's lifespan.
The king said to the Buddha,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me protection and deliverance."
Regarding what was taught— that one should resolve to attain enlightenment, maintain the pure precepts of the Buddha, and cultivate the highest merit—
I shall practice this myself and cause the people of my country to practice this Dharma as well. However,
I do not yet know what kind of mind constitutes "resolving to attain enlightenment."
"What kind of precepts and what kind of merit are most supreme?
I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for me.
The Buddha addressed the Great King, saying:
To "arouse the mind" means to arouse the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
To "uphold the precepts" means to uphold the precept against killing.
To "cultivate superior merit" is not to exceed [the standard] in constructing stūpas.
Out of compassion, they rescue and protect all sentient beings;
various devas and benevolent spirits constantly come to guard them,
never departing from them, just as a shadow follows a form.
It brings forth boundless merit for the Great King.
The merit of the Great King’s establishment of a Buddha-stūpa is inconceivable,
as praised by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
I shall briefly explain the causes and conditions for you, Great King;
you should listen attentively.
In the distant past, there was a young boy who tended cattle here on this very spot.
There were certain physiognomists who came together to examine his marks and said,
"This cowherd boy's life will surely come to an end in seven days.
At another time, this cowherd boy...
He was playing with other children, gathering sand to make toys.
Among them, one child crushed the sand into a mound and said,
"I shall build a Buddha stūpa one span high."
It may be two, three, or up to four finger-widths (*vitasti*).
At that time, this child plays by piling sand into a stupa one finger-width high;
subsequently, his lifespan is further extended by seven years.
While he was gathering sand,
a pratyekabuddha was walking along with his alms bowl;
at that time, the children, with a playful mind, [offered it to him].
Offering the sand, he said, "I give this flour.
Then the Pratyekabuddha extended his bowl and received it;
by means of his supernormal powers, the sand was transformed into flour.
At that time, upon seeing these causes and conditions,
all the children attained pure faith.
Then the Pratyekabuddha bestowed a prophecy upon all the children, speaking thus:
"You youths who have constructed stupas one span high shall,
in a future age, become iron-wheel-turning kings,
ruling over a single world-system."
One who measures two spans becomes a copper-wheel-turning king and rules over two continents;
one who measures three spans becomes a silver-wheel-turning king.
One who rules over three continents and measures four spans [in height] becomes a Golden Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) who rules over the four continents.
At that time, even those children who built such stupas with a playful mind experienced such results;
how much more so for a Great King who has given rise to a heart of utmost sincerity?
If there are sons or daughters of good family...
If one constructs a stūpa according to the Dharma with a resolute mind—
even if it is only the size of one cubit, one span, one finger-joint, or a single grain of barley—
the merit obtained shall be without limit.
Constantly, various devas shower down flowers as an offering.
Therefore, Great King,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to construct a stūpa, [they should do so].
First, one should take the arousal of great compassion toward all sentient beings as the precursor.
With the bodhicitta as the foundation,
one should then purify the ground, construct a mandala, and perform offerings.
Having smeared it with *gomaya*, burned incense, and scattered flowers,
one sits facing directly east and reflects thus:
"The Buddha, the Bhagavat, has perfected the merit of benefiting both himself and others."
Furthermore, it is able to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings.
I have now accomplished the first dharmakāya by generating the bodhicitta,
according to the ritual procedures and rules for constructing stūpas for the Bhagavān.
Perform each step in succession according to the Dharma.
First, gather exquisite flowers and empower them seven times with the dhāraṇī.
Scatter [the offerings] upon the altar to make an offering to the Tathāgata.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Namaḥ samantabhadrapratīcchite supuṣpaketumudrāya tadyathā | puṣpe puṣpe supuṣpe svāhā || Second, when fashioning the lump of clay for the molding:
Perform the visualization of the letter A.
This is the Dharma-realm body of the Tathāgata;
first, one should take refuge by speaking these words:

Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvathāgata-nirghoṣa-svarebhyaḥ | Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvatathāgatānām | Namo ratnatrayāya | Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Namo ratnatrayāya | Namo 'kṣobhyāmitābha-lokeśvara-mahāsthāmaprāpta-bhaiṣajyarāja-gandhahasti-lokeśvara-rājebhyaḥ | When molding [the clay].
By using a koṭi of dhāraṇīs to empower the clay twenty-one times,
one constructs a single Buddha stūpa that is equivalent to constructing a koṭi of Buddha stūpas.
The merit obtained is equal and without distinction.
For this reason, this dhāraṇī is named the Koṭi Dhāraṇī.
The dhāraṇī says:
tadyathā oṃ sukhasvabhāva sukhasvabhāva sukhasvabhāva anutpattidharma dharma dharma dharmatā dharmatā dharmatā.
Tad dhi ni ra ku li ye | Śū va ti | Dhi stu va ti | Sarva-mu-dha | A-dhi-ṣṭhā-na a-dhi-ṣṭhi || 2 ||
*Hanta āmṛte tiṣṭha svāhā*. Third, one should perform the visualization of the syllable *Sphaḥ* upon the clay lump.
One should contemplate this lump of clay as being like crystal,
or like a sphaṭika gem—
pure within and without, distinct, and translucent.
Empower it once with the dhāraṇī. The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajrodātāvabhāsaya svāhā. Fourth, when applying red earth:
One performs the visualization of the color of fire;
thereby, one immediately knows that all mundane and supramundane phenomena are accomplished from subtle atoms.
Having performed this visualization,
take dry red earth and smear it all over the clay ball,
contemplating that all phenomena are primordially unarisen, ultimately empty, and quiescent.
Perform the visualization of the syllable *haṃ*.
Imagine this lump of clay as molten gold,
and then construct the stūpa.
Empower it once with the dhāraṇī. The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ ara-cara-vira-svāhā. Fifth, when placing the clay lump into the mold:
Empower it once with the dhāraṇī,
and then place it in the mold.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ vajradhātu-garbhe svāhā. This is the mantra for entering the Dharmakāya during the sixth stage.
Empower this with the dhāraṇī once.
Then enter into the seal.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ damadhatu ghaṭṭe svāhā. When striking the stūpa with the seal for the seventh time, empower it by reciting this dhāraṇī once.
Then, strike [the drum].
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaga-ra-kuṭa-ya kuṭaya svāhā. This concludes the eighth striking.
When constructing the tiers of the stūpa by hand,
empower each tier once with the dhāraṇī and then install it.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ vajrayuṣe svāhā. Ninth: when the stūpa correctly emerges from the mold.
Empower it once with the dhāraṇī,
and then bring it forth.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ dharmatījuḥ svāhā. When the tenth time has come, having removed the mold from the stūpa and installed the stūpa, [recite this].
Empower it once with the dhāraṇī. The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ subhūtiśrītejo-vajraratna svāhā. For the eleventh time, the placement of the stūpa base is completed.
Pressing the hand upon the top of the stūpa,
empower it once with the dhāraṇī.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
Oṃ pralaṃbha-mātānaye svāhā. (The twelfth time: When placing the parasol upon the stūpa.
Empower it once with this dhāraṇī.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ bharāṇa-ma-a-yu-śe svāhā. The Buddha said to the Great King:
If a son or daughter of good family,
with a pure mind, constructs a Buddhist stūpa according to these ritual procedures—
whether constructing it themselves or instructing others to do so.
Furthermore, if one praises this or accepts it with faith,
the merit obtained will be no different from that of constructing a stūpa for the Buddha;
one should know that such a person, within this very lifetime, [will attain the fruit].
One shall not be struck by any poisons;
one's lifespan will be long and far-reaching, free from untimely death,
and one shall ultimately attain an indestructible body.
All ghosts and spirits dare not approach;
the five planets and seven luminaries follow their commands;
and all enemies are completely dispersed.
In whatever place they are born, their bodies shall always be free from illness;
all sentient beings who see them will rejoice;
and those who lack pure precepts shall become fully endowed with pure precepts.
Those who are unsubdued are made subdued;
those who are impure are made pure;
and for those who have broken their precepts and vows, the precepts and vows are restored.
If one has committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, all such extremely heavy karmic obstacles will be completely extinguished,
and the hindrances and burdens accumulated since beginningless kalpas will be entirely exhausted.
If there are women who desire to conceive a son, [they shall likewise attain their wish].
He shall immediately give birth to a valiant and virtuous son,
whom the Four Great Heavenly Kings will constantly follow and protect.
Such is the merit and blessing of the deed of constructing a stupa.
If a stūpa were to be destroyed and reduced to fine dust,
and a single grain of that dust were blown by the wind and scattered elsewhere,
passing over mountains, forests, rivers, and seas.
All sentient beings who come into contact with these particles shall never again receive a body of mixed species;
from the relinquishing of one body to the taking up of another birth, they shall always behold the Buddha.
Great King, if a son or daughter of good family,
regarding the construction of a stūpa or a dhāraṇī,
visualizes it with clarity and recollects it with single-minded concentration.
They will forever be free from the perils of water, fire, kings, and bandits;
no calamities such as those of war or weapons shall be able to harm them.
Whether in the wilderness or in secluded places, [they shall be safe].
If one is able to proclaim this sutra to the great assembly within a village or a public gathering,
it shall serve as the protection and preservation of the lives of sentient beings.
The measure of the merit obtained is equal to space.
If one were to transcribe and circulate [this text] in a future age,
the merit of doing so would be no different from that of constructing a stūpa, even if the stūpa itself has not yet been built.
For the sake of the Great King and all sentient beings of future ages,
I have extensively expounded upon the merit of constructing stupas for the prolongation of life;
may Your Majesty bear this in mind.
At that time, King Prasenajit and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Translated from the Sanskrit by the Tripitaka Master Muniśrī of Central India.
Written by the Great Virtue of Ximing Monastery, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Yuanzhao;
transmitted by the Great Virtue of Zhangjiao Monastery, the Śramaṇa Jianxu;
proofread once daily by Jingyan over forty-nine years; refined for the text.
